posts.title: Designing resilient payment workflows with Node.js
posts.excerpt: A practical look at idempotency, retries, and event-driven design for financial operations.
posts.body:
> **Example article:** This is starter content for the portfolio. Review and rewrite it in your own voice before launching.

Payment integrations are rarely complicated because of a single API call. They become difficult when requests time out, webhooks arrive twice, and downstream services temporarily disagree.

## Think in states, not requests

Model the operation as an explicit state machine: `initiated → processing → succeeded / failed`. Keep state transitions idempotent, and assign a stable business identifier to each operation.

## Embrace retries carefully

At-least-once delivery is common in queues and webhook systems. Store provider event IDs, use unique indexes to reject duplicates, and make handlers safe to run more than once.

## Keep a trail

Capture correlation IDs and sanitized metadata for every important transition. Logs should help answer *what happened* without exposing secrets.

A good payments backend optimizes first for correctness and recovery, then for throughput.

posts.title: When Redis and queues make a backend simpler
posts.excerpt: Knowing when to reach for asynchronous processing — and when not to.
posts.body:
> **Example article:** This is starter content. Customize it before publishing your site.

Queues can protect user-facing endpoints from slow downstream work. They also introduce operational complexity: retries, dead letters, and observability.

## A good use case

Email delivery, report generation, and event fan-out usually benefit from asynchronous workers. Keep HTTP paths fast and move noncritical work to the background.

## What to monitor

Track processing lag, retry counts, poison messages, and worker health. Set a maximum retry policy and a deliberate dead-letter workflow.

The best architecture isn't the one with the most components — it's the one your team can understand and operate.

posts.title: Building AI features without tying your product to one model
posts.excerpt: Notes on provider adapters, context boundaries, and maintainable LLM integrations.
posts.body:
> **Example article:** Replace this draft with your own experience before going live.

Supporting multiple LLM providers is less about switching endpoint URLs and more about isolating differences in capabilities.

## Build an adapter layer

Define a small internal interface for messages, tools, streaming, and usage metadata. Translate provider-specific request and response shapes at the boundary.

## Treat prompts as product code

Version prompts, test important flows, and keep private context out of logs. Make model errors intelligible to users without leaking internal details.

## Design for graceful degradation

A provider timeout should not cascade into a broken application. Timeouts, quotas, and fallback strategies belong in the core design.
